apps/desktop/src/routes/venue/device-scr.content: This assertion only inspects the returned row, so it cannot detect if `withTransportMode` mutates its argument in place. Since the helper is expected to be pure (the implementation spreads `...row`), the test should also assert the input row is left unchanged; otherwise a refactor to `row.transportMode = mode; return row;` would still pass while breaking aliasing/state assumptions for callers.

The step list is duplicated from `SETUP_EVIDENCE_STEPS` and then cast with `as never`, which disables all type checking on the argument. This means a renamed/removed step in the source model cannot be caught at compile time, and step removal from `SETUP_EVIDENCE_STEPS` would leave this test green even though the `next === "ready"` contract changed. Import the exported constant instead of hardcoding/casting.

This `toEqual(["dj", "controller"])` asserts exact array order, coupling the test to the implementation's iteration order (`SETUP_EVIDENCE_STEPS.filter(...)`) rather than to the semantic contract (both steps done, no others). It also never verifies `next` for the partial case. Prefer order-independent membership checks and assert the `next` value for the partial state.

Only a single fully-populated, healthy `online` tile with `segments > 0` is exercised, so the qualification/measurement edge cases that actually drive `latencySource`/`segments` are untested: e.g. `qualified: true` with `segments === 0` (implementation returns `segments: null` while `qualifiedResolution` reports "0 segments"), and non-online/degraded health. Adding a zero-segment qualified fixture would pin the `qualified && tile.segments > 0` branch and surface that inconsistency.

apps/desktop/src/routes/venue/room-previ.content: `referenceById(roomId)` throws for any id that is not present in `REFERENCE_ROOMS` (`if (!found) throw new Error(...)` in packages/venue/src/reference.ts). The result is dereferenced immediately (`ref.room`, `ref.zeroS`, `ref.runs`), so a mistyped/misconfigured `roomId` (e.g. the future wizard passing a user/non-reference room id) will crash the whole venue route during render instead of degrading gracefully. Look up the room safely (or wrap in try/catch) and render an empty/fallback preview when the id is unknown.

The `useMemo` depends on `beat`, so `referenceById`, `fieldCellsForReference` and `computeFields` — all of which depend only on `roomId` and allocate large typed arrays (see computeFields) — are recomputed on every beat tick even though only `sampleSpatial` actually consumes `beat`. Since `beat` is driven by the numeric input, this re-runs all the static field math on each keystroke/step. Split this into a memo keyed on `[roomId]` that produces `{ cells, fields }`, then a second cheap memo keyed on `[built, beat]` that only maps `sampleSpatial` over the cells.

The `min`/`max` attributes on the input are declarative only and do not constrain typed or programmatically set values; `onChange` maps only `NaN` (via `Number(...) || 0`) to 0, so negative or `> 16` beats pass straight into `sampleSpatial`. Clamp the parsed value to the declared range before storing it, e.g. `const v = Number(e.target.value); setBeat(Number.isFinite(v) ? Math.min(16, Math.max(0, v)) : 0)` (or use `e.currentTarget.validity.valid`).

The preview overrides the room's own configuration: `perimeterDirection` is hardcoded to `"clockwise"` and the Orbit `params` (`heads`, `beatsPerRevolution`, `tailCells`, `tailCurve`, `phase`) are fixed constants. If the referenced room is counter-clockwise (or the caller expects the real primitive params), the preview silently disagrees with the actual venue configuration. At minimum, derive direction from `ref.room.perimeterDirection` and document that the sampling params are preview-only placeholders.
apps/desktop/src/routes/venue/room-previ.existing_code: const room = { ...ref.room, logicalZeroS: ref.zeroS, perimeterDirection: "clockwise" as const };

apps/desktop/vite.config.ts.content:
The subpath regex `^@autolight\/([^/]+)\/([^/]+)$` matches exactly one flat segment and hardcodes the `.ts` extension. Consequences:
1. A deeper import such as `@autolight/pkg/sub/module` does NOT match, so `resolve.alias` falls through to the next entry — the **string-form barrel alias**. Vite/`@rollup/plugin-alias` replaces string matches by prefix, so `@autolight/pkg/sub/module` becomes `.../pkg/src/index.ts/sub/module`: a bogus path that only fails at bundle time. That is precisely the fall-through the surrounding comment says this block prevents.
2. Subpath modules that are `.tsx`, or subdirectories whose entry is `index.ts`, can never resolve because `$2.ts` is forced.
Consider allowing nested segments and letting Vite's extension resolution handle the leaf, e.g. `find: /^@autolight\/([^/]+)\/(.+)$/` with `replacement: join(workspaceSrc, "$1", "src", "$2")`.

`readdirSync(workspaceSrc)` is called without `withFileTypes`, so every entry (including non-directories such as a stray `.DS_Store`, README, or lock file) becomes an alias, and no check is made that `<pkg>/src/index.ts` actually exists. A package directory that hasn't added a barrel yet, or any file entry, therefore produces a dangling `@autolight/<entry>` alias that only surfaces later as a confusing "failed to resolve import" at module load. Filter to entries that are directories and verify `join(workspaceSrc, p, "src", "index.ts")` exists before adding the alias.

These `execSync` git calls run synchronously at config-load time with no `timeout` and default `maxBuffer`; a git that hangs (index.lock contention, slow network filesystem) blocks the entire Vite startup. The bare `catch` also swallows every failure, so a genuinely broken git invocation is indistinguishable from "not a git checkout" and silently ships `sha: "unknown"` — defeating the stated goal of proving which commit is running. Pass `{ cwd: root, timeout: <ms>, maxBuffer: <bytes> }` and at least warn once when the lookup fails.
apps/desktop/vite.config.ts.existing_code: sha = execSync("git rev-parse --short HEAD", { cwd: root }).toString().trim();

apps/desktop/vite.config.ts.content: `fs.allow` is widened to the monorepo root (`join(root, "..", "..")`), so the dev server will serve any file in the repository — including `.env`/credential files and unrelated apps — to anything that can reach `localhost:5173`. Restrict the allow list to the renderer root plus only the aliased package `src` directories that are actually needed (e.g. `join(workspaceSrc, "*")` or the resolved package src paths), rather than the whole repo.
apps/desktop/vite.config.ts.existing_code: server: { port: 5173, strictPort: true, fs: { allow: [join(root, "..", "..")] } },

packages/analysis-client/package.json.content: The build compiles test files into the published output. `tsconfig.json` includes `"src"` with no `exclude`, and `tsconfig.base.json` sets `declaration: true`/`sourceMap: true`, so `tsc -p tsconfig.json` emits `dist/index.test.js`, `dist/index.test.d.ts`, etc. Those emitted files import `vitest`, which is declared only as a devDependency, so any consumer (or bundler/CI that traverses `dist/**`) will hit an unresolved `vitest` import. Exclude test files from the build (e.g. add `"exclude": ["src/**/*.test.ts"]` to tsconfig.json, or use a dedicated `tsconfig.build.json`).

`main`/`types` point into `dist`, but there is no `files` (or `exports`) field. The publish payload is therefore governed by ignore files, and the repo `.gitignore` ignores `dist/` — so a packed/published tarball can omit `dist/index.js` while `main`/`types` still reference it, producing ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND for consumers. Add an explicit allowlist, e.g. `"files": ["dist"]` (combined with excluding tests from the build), and add `"private": true` if this package is not meant to be published.

`--passWithNoTests` makes the test gate succeed when no tests are collected (broken globs, deleted/renamed test files, or misconfigured vitest), silently masking a missing or non-running suite in CI. Consider dropping the flag (or asserting a minimum test count) so an empty run fails.

`lint` is identical to `typecheck`, so the `lint` script performs no linting and cannot catch anything beyond type errors. Either wire it to the actual linter used by the repo (oxlint/eslint) or remove the duplicate script to avoid a misleading lint gate.

packages/ble/src/provisioning.test.ts.content: The reassembled byte check truncates with `slice(0, expectedPayload.length)`, so any extra bytes written beyond the expected payload (an over-send bug) are silently discarded and the test still passes. Compare the full received buffer so both over- and under-send are caught.

`chunks.map(() => 0xa1)` is derived from `chunks` itself, so the assertion only checks every decoded frame equals 0xa1 — it never validates that the number of chunk frames, or the per-chunk payload offsets/ordering, match the encoded payload. An extra or missing chunk frame (e.g. a duplicated or dropped chunk with identical proType/cmd but wrong offset) would go undetected here. Assert the expected chunk count and decode each chunk payload against `bleProvisionChunks(expectedPayload)`.

The fake clock is inconsistent: `write` advances the simulated time by a hardcoded 300 ms while `sleep` only records the value and never advances time, so the simulator's timeline does not reflect the 3 s start wait or the 300 ms pacing actually requested. Any sim behaviour that depends on `now` (e.g. `budgetHz` rate limiting, which is currently disabled with `budgetHz: null`) would pass or fail for the wrong reason. Wire the clock to the recorded sleeps so the sim timeline mirrors the real flow.

Only happy paths are covered: no test exercises a rejected/failed transport `write`, an aborted transfer, or an `onPasswordSaved` that throws. As a result, `provisionBleWifi`'s error propagation and any stop/cleanup guarantees on failure are unverified, even though the transfer is security-sensitive. Add a failure-path case asserting rejection and that no further frames are written after a mid-transfer failure.

packages/ble/src/sim.test.ts.content: This assertion is vacuous and cannot detect regressions. `simContractChecks` builds checks whose pass conditions are trivially true: `host-color-hold` only asserts `typeof p.hostColorHeld(now) === "boolean"` (always a boolean regardless of `now`, so the passed `999` is irrelevant), and `one-connection-rule` is `peripherals.every((p) => !p.connected || ...)` which is satisfied vacuously because `simFamilyPeripherals()` never connects any peripheral (`!p.connected` is true for all). So `checks.every((c) => c.ok)` will be true even if host-colour hold or the one-connection rule is completely broken. Drive real state (connect a peripheral, apply a host colour and probe the hold) or assert on the meaningful state rather than only the boolean `ok` flags.

The clock is frozen at 1000, so both `write` calls carry the same timestamp and the stall is produced by a zero-length inter-write gap rather than by exhaustion of the time-window budget. Consequently the 1000 ms window filter (`this.writeTimes.filter((t) => now - t < 1000)`) and the `stalledUntil` recovery path are never exercised, and `expect(peripheral.metrics.stalled).toBeGreaterThan(0)` would still pass if that window logic regressed. Use a mutable clock that advances between writes (e.g. write, advance comfortably past the spacing, write again) and assert which specific frame was dropped/acked.
packages/ble/src/sim.test.ts.existing_code: const adapter = new SimBleAdapter({ kind: "noble", clock: () => 1000 });

packages/ble/src/sim.test.ts.content: `17`/`19` are magic offsets that encode the 17-byte frame payload padding rather than the chunk data: `answerProvision` pushes `payload.slice(0, 17)`, so `simProvisionBytes` concatenates padded chunks and the second chunk starts at 17 purely because of the trailing zeros of the first. The test therefore cannot detect padding-related corruption (e.g. per-write trailing zero bytes being stored) and would silently change meaning if chunk storage ever stopped padding. Assert the chunk boundaries explicitly (e.g. inspect `peripheral.provisioned[0]`/`[1]` or a documented chunk-length constant) instead of hard-coding 17/19.

The decoded host colour is only asserted non-null; the sub/payload bytes are never compared with the input `{ r: 9, g: 9, b: 9 }`, and `painted[0]` alone does not prove the RGB order is correct (a swapped channel would still pass for equal values). Also the hold boundary is probed only at 9001, leaving the exact `7000 + renderHoldMs = 9000` boundary untested, so an off-by-one in `hostColorHeld` (`now - hostColorAt < hold`) could go unnoticed. Assert the decoded payload equals `[0x83, 9, 9, 9]` and probe `hostColorHeld(9000)`.

packages/cloud/src/cross-check.test.ts.content: Weak assertion: `toContain("14")`/`toContain("20")` only verifies the two digits appear somewhere in the note. The model is "H6076" and the hardwareId contains no "14"/"20", so the test passes even if the note labels the values backwards (e.g. "Cloud declares 14 ... measured 20"). A broken or misleading note format therefore goes undetected. Assert the full note (or at least the labeled substrings "declares 20" and "measured 14").

The hand-built mock bypasses the real client shape: `parseDeviceEntry` derives `declaredSegmentCount` from `properties` (`segments`/`segmentCount`/`zoneCount`, floored, `>0`). Tests 1 and 2 feed this literal directly into `crossCheckQualification`, and test 3 only exercises the `null` path. As a result, no test drives a real parsed non-null count into the cross-check, so a regression in `parseDeviceEntry` (renamed/removed key, wrong flooring) leaves the entire "disagree" path passing. Add a case that parses `{ ...properties: { zoneCount: 20 } }` and feeds the result into `crossCheckQualification` expecting "disagree".

`mismatchRecorded` is asserted only as the boolean returned by `crossCheckQualification`. Nothing verifies the mismatch is actually persisted/emitted downstream, and `crossCheckQualification` currently has no non-test consumer (only re-exported from index.ts). The test therefore cannot distinguish a real record from a flag that is never written to device evidence, leaving the "records a mismatch" claim unverified. Either assert the persisted evidence artifact or document that the flag is the contract.

Boundary coverage is missing: `compareDeclaredSegments`/`crossCheckQualification` are never exercised with declared values of 0, negative, or non-integer, nor with a non-finite/NaN count (e.g. `compareDeclaredSegments(NaN, NaN)` returns "disagree" since `NaN === NaN` is false). Note `parseDeviceEntry` maps `0`/negative to `null` (silent), so a cloud declaring "0 segments" flows as silent rather than disagree — worth a test to pin the intended behavior.
